title: TC0-09555
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): She is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated July 10, 2020, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of China. She is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated July 10, 2020, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.

I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The determinative issue is credibility. No new evidence was presented, and no oral hearing was convened.

The Appellant alleges that she was introduced to Christianity by her friend when she was experiencing difficulties in her marriage due to her husband's drinking. In late XXXX 2017, the Appellant alleges she went to a house church for the first time and she continued to attend church services every Sunday thereafter. On XXXX XXXX, 2018, she alleges that three fellow believers were detained by the PSB (Public Security Bureau) while they were spreading religious flyers and the following day, the group leader was taken into custody. Those arrested revealed the names of the church members to the PSB. On XXXX XXXX, 2018, the Appellant alleges that three village committee officers went to the Appellant's home and questioned her. She was threatened that she would be arrested and sent to jail if she continued to participate in any illegal religious activities. The Appellant left China with the assistance of a snakehead and arrived in Toronto on XXXX XXXX, 2018. The Appellant alleges that she fears persecution from the Chinese authorities due to her religious practice and that she will not be able to practice her faith freely.

My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 The RPD made numerous negative credibility inferences and ultimately determined that the Appellant was not a follower of the Christian faith and that, should she return to China she would not practice. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its assessment of her credibility and her religious identity, her sur place claim, and in its failure to assess her supporting documentation. After conducting an independent review of the record, I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant is not a practicing Christian. The Appellant did not credibly establish her religious profile
The Appellant has argued that the RPD conducted a microscopic analysis and that the RPD did not consider her lack of education or nervousness.

The Appellant is elementary school educated, and a married mother of two children. She testified to being introduced to Christianity in China by her friend, in XXXX of 2017, and that she was of the Pentecostal denomination.2 The Appellant was asked by the RPD how she practiced her faith and she replied that at home she read the Bible, prayed, and worshipped God.3 The Appellant also testified that in China she attended house church every Sunday from late XXXX 2017 until early XXXX 2018.4 The services lasted over an hour, during which she and fellow church members would pray, sing hymns and share testimonies. The evidence shows that the Appellant was given a Bible as a welcoming gift on her first visit to the church in XXXX 2017, and that she testified to reading the Bible 2-3 times per week while in China.5

In Canada, the Appellant testified that she continued to practice her faith. She stated that she attended church on Sundays where she would read the Bible and sing hymns.6 The Appellant presented a letter from the XXXX XXXX XXXX, that stated she had been attending there since XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 and had taken an interest in studying Bible class.7 She also stated that she would attend church on Tuesdays when the pastor would preach. In addition, she volunteered at the church by greeting newcomers and cleaning up and putting away the chairs at the end of services. The Appellant testified that on two occasions she gave out brochures to the public.8 In Canada, the Appellant testified that she continues to read the Bible 2-3 times per week. She testified that the books of Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, and Revelations were from the Old Testament and that Genesis, Romans, and Exodus were from the New Testament. The Appellant stated that she celebrated Easter Sunday, Good Friday, the Pentecost, and Christmas.9 The Appellant testified that she was baptized in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2018. The record shows that the Appellant had attended weekly church services for approximately two years and XXXX months at the time of her hearing and had been reading from the Bible 2-3 times per week for the same period of time.

The RPD questioned the Appellant about her most recent church attendance, and the Appellant testified that it took place two days prior to the hearing. When asked by the RPD what part of the Bible was read during the service, the Appellant replied that the Reverend was talking about the precious blood of Jesus. When asked to explain the service, the Appellant stated that Jesus was crucified on the cross and that he used his precious blood to redeem people.10 She then testified that she did not understand the rest of the sermon, when asked why,11 she replied that she has little education and a poor memory. The Appellant was again asked what part of the Bible was read during the service, she replied that she was nervous but did not provide a response. I do not find the Appellant's response to be credible. The Appellant was able to recall in her testimony the date and day of the week that her fellow church members were arrested by the PSB in China in 2018, yet she could not remember what the service she attended two days prior was about and what part of the Bible was read. The Appellant has not provided any corroborating documentation, such as a medical or psychological report that would indicate that she suffers from memory or mental health problems. The record does show that the Appellant stated during her testimony that she was nervous, but the RPD dealt with the matter appropriately, telling the Appellant not to worry and to take her time. Further, the Appellant was able to respond to other questions that were asked at the hearing and, again, she provided no documentation regarding medical or psychological problems. The record also shows that some questions that were put to the Appellant went unanswered, contrary to her argument that she responded fully and accurately to every question. The Appellant testified that she would not give up her faith as she had received peace since becoming a Christian. The Appellant claims a strong conviction to her faith; she has spent a significant amount of time reading the Bible, she has taken an interest in Bible study and has attended weekly services for over two years, yet she lacked knowledge of a service held just two days prior. Her lack of knowledge in this regard is not compatible with her practice, accordingly, I draw a negative inference.

The record shows that the RPD asked the Appellant general questions about how she practiced her faith, the meaning of baptism and the Pentecost, and the books of the Bible. The Appellant has not directed me to any examples of microscopic analysis. I do not find that the RPD conducted a microscopic analysis as the Appellant has submitted.

The RPD made a negative inference as to the Appellant's credibility because she could not provide any details about her baptismal classes. The Appellant provided a baptismal certificate,12 and testified that the meaning of baptism was that going into the water represents death and coming out represents life.13 She also testified that in order to be baptized she first had to get a baptism license by attending six baptismal classes. When asked what she learned in these classes the Appellant stated that she did not remember.14 The Appellant has again argued that she suffers from a poor memory. I do not find this a credible argument. As above, the Appellant has demonstrated an ability to remember details from her past and there is no evidence of any medical reason for a poor memory. The Appellant made a conscious decision to get baptized at age 43, she was not baptized at birth or at a young age, this was a recent and significant demonstration of her faith. I find that the Appellant's inability to remember anything she learned from six classes she attended a year prior about something so meaningful to her impugns her credibility.

The RPD did not find it reasonable that the Appellant could not name further books in the Bible and could not explain what is found in the book of Exodus. The Appellant argues that the RPD erroneously imposed a knowledge test and that it erred in its assessment of her sincerity of faith. I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred in finding it unreasonable that she was unable to name further books in the Bible. The RPD asked the Appellant to name some books from the New Testament, the Appellant provided five. When asked to name books from the Old Testament the Appellant replied Genesis, Romans, and Exodus.15 Later the RPD asked the Appellant if she knew any other books from the Bible and the Appellant repeated the same ones she previously cited. There are over sixty books in the Bible, some of which are relatively obscure. It is not unreasonable that on the spur of the moment the Appellant could not name further books. This was an error by the RPD.

With regard to Exodus, the RPD finding that it was unreasonable that the Appellant was unable to testify as to its contents was not in error. Here, the RPD was not engaging in a knowledge test. The Appellant listed the book of Exodus when asked by the RPD about books of the Bible. The Appellant testified that she reads the Bible 2-3 times per week and her Reverend wrote that she took an interest in Bible study. The book of Exodus is the second book in the Bible and contains the Ten Commandments and the parting of the Red Sea. These are two of the most popular Christian stories, known even by many non-Christians, given the Appellant's alleged commitment to the study of the Bible, it is not reasonable that she could not describe its contents. I make a negative credibility inference as a result.

The RPD made a negative inference as to the Appellant's credibility because despite being an alleged follower of the Pentecostal denomination of Christianity the Appellant was unaware when the Pentecost was observed the year prior. The Appellant argues although she initially testified that she could not remember she eventually provided an accurate response. She also argues that the RPD relied only on her inability to answer the question and did not further question her on the significance of the Pentecost.

A review of the record shows that the Appellant testified that she was of the Pentecostal denomination, and that since XXXX 2018, she has been attending a Pentecostal church on a weekly basis. When asked if she celebrated any holidays, the Appellant testified the Pentecostal day along with Easter and Christmas.16 Contrary to the Appellant's argument that the RPD did not question her on the significance of the Pentecost, the record shows that the RPD asked the Appellant to explain the significance of the Pentecost twice. The Appellant first testified the significance was that the disciples were filled with the holy spirit so they could speak a tongue.17 The RPD asked her to explain the importance of that to the faith and the Appellant testified that when people are filled with the holy spirit some of them are writing, some of them are laughing, some people speak different dialects.18 The Pentecost takes place on the seventh Sunday following Easter and historically is viewed as the birth of the church. In 2019, the Pentecost was on June 9. The Appellant first testified that the date of Pentecost is May 22. When asked by the RPD when the Pentecost was observed in 2019 the Appellant testified that she did not remember, then testified that it was on April 19.19 The Appellant did not provide an accurate response as she has submitted. Many Christians would be unaware of the date of the Pentecost, but the Appellant claims to be Pentecostal, and testified that the Pentecost was one of the three religious holidays that she celebrated, yet she could not identify the date of the Pentecost some seven months earlier. I make a negative inference as to her credibility.

The Appellant has argued that the RPD left out part of her testimony with regards to the significance of Easter and baptism to portray her in an ingenuine light. The record shows that when asked about the significance of Easter the Appellant first replied, 'three days later, according to the Jewish calendar March 21st, that's their first Sunday.'20 This response is unintelligible, and the RPD asked her again. She replied that Jesus Christ was nailed on the cross and three days later he was alive.21 The Appellant did testify to the meaning of Easter, but the response was general in nature, lacking in detail, and confusing. Similarly, her testimony about the meaning or significance of the Pentecost was void of any detail or connection to the sincerity of her faith. The RPD did not ignore evidence of the Appellant's faith. The Appellant's supporting documents are afforded little weight

The RPD assigned little weight to the Appellant's baptismal certificate and her supporting letters. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by allocating no weight to her supporting documents and for not providing sufficient reasons for the assigned weight.

The record shows that the RPD assigned little value, not no weight as the Appellant has submitted; to the letters of support from the Appellant's husband,22 and the husband of her friend.23 The RPD states that the letters had no accompanying identification, were not sworn, and the authors were not produced as witnesses. I find that the RPD erred in assigning little weight simply because the documents were not sworn. There is no requirement that the Appellant produce only sworn documents. Presumably the authors could not attend at a hearing and thus the need for the letters.

However, after an independent assessment, I assign the letters little weight. The letters are predominantly a summary of the events from the arrests on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, until the Appellant left China on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. Both letters contain a short sentence attesting that the Appellant is a Christian, this is confirmation of what the Appellant has testified to. The letters do not provide any insight as to the sincerity of her faith.

Similarly, I have assigned little weight to the letter from the Reverend XXXX24 and the Appellant's baptismal certificate. I find that the letter and the baptismal certificate can only attest to her participation in church activities, they do not speak to her motivation. This letter, too, summarizes the Appellant's narrative and then provides advocacy based on the author's own experiences in China. I give little evidentiary weight to the documents in assessing the genuineness of her religious faith.

Given the above, I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that she is a genuine follower of the Pentecostal faith. The Appellant is not a convention refugee sur place

The RPD determined that the Appellant's practice of her faith in Canada was not genuine, but made to advance her claim, and should she return to China she would not practice the faith. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in its assessment of the sur place aspect of her claim, that if there is credible evidence supporting the Appellant's religious activities in Canada that are likely to risk harm to her if returned to her home country, the RPD must consider the sur place aspect.

I have conducted my own assessment of the sur place aspect of the claim and find that there is no evidence in the record that the Appellant's religious activities in Canada have come to the attention of the Chinese authorities. The record shows that the Appellant attends XXXX XXXX XXXX church services weekly. The Appellant also testified that on two occasions she and fellow church members gave out religious brochures on the streets. There is no evidence on the record that the Chinese authorities monitor the XXXX XXXX XXXX, I find that the Appellant's attendance at the church has not come to the attention of the Chinese authorities. I also find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant would not practice her religion if returned to China, given that she is not a genuine Christian. The hearing was procedurally fair

The Appellant has argued that she answered all questions put to her by the RPD and that she was not informed that her lack of detail would be a factor in her claim, as such the hearing lacked procedural fairness. I do not agree. The burden of proof rests with the claimant, she has to put forth her best evidence. When the Appellant testified that she could not remember what the service two days prior to the hearing was about, or what she learned in her baptismal classes, or what the book of Exodus was about, there was little more that the RPD could do. It was not an error for the RPD not to ask further questions here, the Appellant testified that she did not know or remember. The Appellant testified that her favorite story of the Bible was that of Adam and Eve, yet the RPD asked her twice where that story was found in the Bible and the Appellant said she was nervous but never provided a reply.25 After listening to the audio recording of the hearing, I find that the hearing was procedurally fair.

I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that she is a genuine practitioner of the Christian faith. I find that the Appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution on the basis of her religion should she return to China.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. (signed) Ron Stratigopoulos R.
